name: Winchester Cathedral
summary: The cathedral and Benedictine priory of St Swithun at Winchester, begun by Bishop Walkelin in 1079 beside the Anglo-Saxon Old and New Minsters, where the mixed bones of West Saxon and Danish kings lie in mortuary chests and the Winchester Bible is kept.
overview: Winchester Cathedral replaced the Old Minster, burial church of the West Saxon kings, with a Norman church begun in 1079. It kept Swithun's shrine and the bones of kings from Egbert to Cnut and William II in chests whose contents are now mixed, and its fabric runs from Walkelin's transepts to William of Wykeham's recased nave.
knownFor: Site of the Anglo-Saxon Old Minster and New Minster
Mortuary chests naming Cnut the Great, Emma of Normandy and William II of England

imageInfo.creator: Michael van der Gucht (signed as engraver)
imageInfo.note: The dedication names Jonathan Trelawny, bishop of Winchester from 1707 to 1721, so the plate was probably engraved during his episcopate, nearly two centuries after the Middle Ages. It shows the medieval church from the north: the Lady Chapel at the east end on the left, Walkelin's Norman transept and low tower, and the long Perpendicular nave ending in the west front. Roofs and pinnacles are drawn schematically. The Codex copy is cropped to remove the blank border of the source scan (owner rule: no margins around images).

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Winchester Cathedral stands in the south-east quarter of Winchester, on low ground near the River Itchen where the West Saxon kings built their first church. The present building, begun by Bishop Walkelin in 1079, replaced two Anglo-Saxon churches that stood immediately to its north, the Old Minster and the New Minster, and inherited their saints and their royal dead. About 170 metres from end to end, it is one of the longest medieval churches in Europe.

For most of the Middle Ages it was also a Benedictine monastery, the priory of St Swithun, whose monks served the cathedral under the bishop. Its fabric records three great campaigns: Walkelin's transepts and crypt, the Early English retrochoir begun in 1202, and the nave that William of Wykeham recased in the Perpendicular style from 1394. Its bishops were among the richest men in England, and the chantry chapels they built for themselves still crowd the east end.

contentSections.title: The Old Minster and the New Minster
paragraphs: The first church, later called the Old Minster, stood just north of the present nave. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle credits King Cenwalh with building it in 648, but that entry was written two centuries later, and the church may date instead from about 660, when the West Saxon bishop's seat moved from Dorchester-on-Thames under Bishop Wine. Bishop Æthelwold, who held the see from 963 to 984, rebuilt it on a vast scale, extending it west over the place of Swithun's first grave and adding an apse over an eastern crypt; the enlarged church was dedicated in 980 and again in 993 or 994.

Edward the Elder founded the New Minster in 901 so close to the north side that later writers said the chanting of the two communities ran together. It carried out a plan of Alfred the Great, whose body was moved into it. In 964 Æthelwold, backed by Edgar the Peaceful, expelled the secular canons from both churches and installed monks. The New Minster's book of benefactors, the Liber Vitae of about 1031, opens with a drawing of Cnut the Great and Emma of Normandy placing a gold cross on its altar. That community left in 1110 for Hyde Abbey outside the walls, and excavations by Martin Biddle and Birthe Kjølbye-Biddle between 1962 and 1969 recovered the Old Minster's plan, now marked out in brick in the grass north of the cathedral.

contentSections.title: Swithun's shrine
paragraphs: Swithun was bishop from 852 until his death in 863 and, according to William of Malmesbury, asked to be buried outside the church, where passers-by would tread on his grave and rain from the eaves would fall on it. More than a century later Æthelwold made him patron of the reformed cathedral, and on 15 July 971 his bones were carried inside amid reports of cures. A story told at Winchester has the monks so worn out by being called to give thanks for miracles several times a night that the saint had to rebuke them in a vision. The relics were later divided: his head went to Canterbury and an arm to Peterborough.

The shrine drew pilgrims for more than five centuries. On 15 July 1093 it was carried in procession from the Old Minster into Walkelin's church, and in the later Middle Ages it stood in the retrochoir behind the high altar, where pilgrims could crawl into a low passage beneath the relic platform known as the Holy Hole. Two famous stories are later growths: the legend that Queen Emma proved her chastity by walking over red-hot ploughshares under Swithun's protection first appears in the thirteenth century, and the saying that rain on St Swithun's day brings forty days of rain cannot be traced before the seventeenth. Henry VIII's commissioners Thomas Wriothesley and Richard Pollard broke up the shrine in September 1538.

contentSections.title: Kings in the Old Minster
paragraphs: The Old Minster was the chief burial church of the West Saxon dynasty. Egbert of Wessex was buried at Winchester in 839, and the remains of his son Æthelwulf of Wessex, first buried at Steyning, were later brought there. Alfred the Great lay in the Old Minster from 899 until his move to the New Minster, and Eadred of England was buried there in 955, perhaps not where his will shows he had wished to lie. Cnut the Great, who gave the church a shrine for the relics of St Birinus, was buried there in 1035, followed by his son Harthacnut in 1042, his widow Emma in 1052 and Earl Godwin in 1053.

The church was also a stage for royal ceremony. Edward the Confessor was crowned in the Old Minster on 3 April 1043. Later that year he rode back to Winchester with the earls Leofric, Godwin and Siward, accused his mother of treason and stripped her of her lands and treasure, which he soon restored. Queen Emma then lived out her life beside the minster, and her burial next to Cnut and Harthacnut made the church the resting place of the whole Danish royal family in England.

contentSections.title: Walkelin's Norman cathedral
paragraphs: Walkelin, a royal chaplain from Normandy and probably a former canon of Rouen, became bishop in 1070 after papal legates deposed Stigand at a council in Winchester. In 1079 he began a new cathedral immediately south of the Old Minster, built of limestone brought from Quarr on the Isle of Wight and of stone taken from the old church. The Annals of Winchester tell how William the Conqueror granted him as much timber from a royal wood as his carpenters could take in three or four days, and how Walkelin brought in so many carpenters that the whole wood was felled, and had to beg the angry king's pardon.

In 1093 the monks moved into the finished eastern parts; on 15 July they brought Swithun's shrine across, and the next day Walkelin's workmen began pulling the Old Minster down. His church was more than 150 metres long, and its transepts and crypt survive almost as he left them, with massive piers, three storeys of round arches and aisles on both sides of each arm. The central tower collapsed in 1107, and William of Malmesbury reported that some blamed the burial beneath it of William II of England, killed unconfessed in the New Forest in 1100. It was rebuilt low and plain, and the nave was completed under Bishop William Giffard, who died in 1129.

contentSections.title: The royal bones and the mortuary chests
paragraphs: The kings and bishops of the Old Minster were exhumed in 1093 or soon after and reburied in the new church. In 1158 Bishop Henry of Blois moved their bones from what a chronicler called an unseemly place into lead coffers near the high altar, and the same writer complained that kings had been mixed with bishops. In the early sixteenth century, traditionally under Bishop Richard Fox, the remains were placed in painted wooden chests set on top of the new stone screens around the presbytery, where the chests still stand.

In December 1642 Parliamentarian soldiers ransacked the cathedral, threw the chests down and scattered the bones across the pavement; an account printed in 1685 says they hurled them at windows they could not reach with their swords. Four chests survived, two replacements were made in 1662, and the bones were gathered up and put back with no way of telling whose they were. The six chests now carry Latin names for Cynegils, Cynewulf, Egbert, Æthelwulf, Eadred, Edmund, Cnut, William Rufus, the bishops Wine and Ælfwine, and Queen Emma. Harthacnut, named in the 1642 account, may also lie among them, and no chest can be trusted to hold the people painted on it.

Scientific study began with the conservation of the chests in 2012. Radiocarbon dates obtained with the University of Oxford in 2015 showed that the bones belong to the Anglo-Saxon and early Norman centuries rather than to later burials. A University of Bristol team led by Kate Robson Brown sorted more than 1,300 bones into at least 23 partial skeletons, where no more than fifteen people had been expected, and in May 2019 announced the scattered remains of a mature woman who could be Emma of Normandy, and of two unrecorded boys aged between 10 and 15 who died between the mid-eleventh and late twelfth centuries. In January 2026 the cathedral began returning the bones to the chests grouped by radiocarbon date, with the identifications still to be published.

contentSections.title: Henry of Blois and the Winchester Bible
paragraphs: Henry of Blois, grandson of William the Conqueror and brother of Stephen of England, was bishop from 1129 to 1171 and the cathedral's greatest patron after Walkelin. Besides gathering the royal bones, he is credited with the black Tournai marble font carved with the miracles of St Nicholas, one of about ten such fonts imported into England, and he was probably the patron of the Winchester Bible. The Purbeck marble tomb in the choir long shown as that of William Rufus is now thought more likely to be his.

The Bible, made in the priory between about 1150 and 1175, is the largest surviving English Bible of the twelfth century: 468 leaves of calfskin, each about 58 by 40 centimetres, written out by a single scribe. Its initials are the work of at least six artists, whom Walter Oakeshott named in 1945 after their best-known pages, among them the Master of the Leaping Figures and the Master of the Morgan Leaf. They used gold and ultramarine ground from Afghan lapis lazuli, and because the decoration was never finished, underdrawing, gilding and paint can be seen at different stages on the same page. One leaf, probably removed at a rebinding in 1820, was bought by John Pierpont Morgan in 1912 and is now in the Morgan Library in New York.

A story in the Life of St Hugh of Lincoln tells how Henry II took a splendid new Bible from the monks of St Swithun for his Carthusian house at Witham, and how Hugh, learning where it had come from, quietly returned it. Many historians identify that book with this manuscript, although the story does not describe it closely enough to be sure.

contentSections.title: Gothic bishops and royal occasions
paragraphs: The Norman apse was the first part to go. Bishop Godfrey de Lucy began a low retrochoir in the Early English style in 1202 to give pilgrims room around the shrine, and it was finished after his death in 1204. Wykeham's predecessor, bishop from 1346 to 1366, began rebuilding the west end. William of Wykeham took on the nave in 1394 with his master mason William Wynford: instead of demolishing Walkelin's arcades, they cased the Norman piers in new stone, merged arcade and gallery into two tall storeys and covered the nave with a stone vault. The work went on until about 1420, and Wykeham was buried in 1404 in a chantry chapel set between two of the piers he had remodelled.

His successors lined the east end with chantries, each served by a priest saying Masses for the bishop's soul: Henry Beaufort, cardinal and half-brother of Henry IV of England, who died in 1447; William Waynflete, founder of Magdalen College, Oxford, who died in 1486; and Richard Fox, who died in 1528 after rebuilding the presbytery and its screens. The stone reredos behind the high altar, carved between about 1450 and 1476, was filled with statues that were torn out at the Reformation. The crown used the church too: Richard the Lionheart wore his crown there in April 1194 after his release from captivity, and Henry IV married Joan of Navarre there on 7 February 1403.

The priory surrendered to Henry VIII in 1539 and was refounded as a dean and chapter, with the last prior, William Basyng, as the first dean. Mary I married Philip of Spain in the cathedral in July 1554. The cloister and chapter house were demolished later in the century, and after the destruction of 1642 the shattered glass of the great west window was set back as a random mosaic in the 1660s, as it remains.

sectionImages.caption: The north side of Winchester Cathedral, with Walkelin's Norman transept and tower on the left and the recased nave and west front on the right, photographed in 2006.
sectionImages.creator: Antony McCallum (WyrdLight)
sectionImages.note: Modern photograph. The transept with its round-headed windows and the squat tower rebuilt after 1107 are Norman work; the nave keeps Walkelin's core inside the Perpendicular casing begun in 1394, and the great west window belongs to the fourteenth-century west front.

sectionImages.section: The royal bones and the mortuary chests
sectionImages.caption: Three of the six painted mortuary chests on the stone screen beside the presbytery of Winchester Cathedral, photographed in 2022.
sectionImages.creator: BabelStone
sectionImages.date: photograph, 2022 (screens and chests of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries)
sectionImages.note: Modern photograph. The screens and the older chests belong to the early sixteenth century, traditionally to Bishop Richard Fox; four chests survived the Parliamentarian attack of 1642 and two were made in 1662 to replace lost ones. The names painted on them do not reliably match the bones inside.

sectionImages.section: Henry of Blois and the Winchester Bible
sectionImages.caption: An initial from the Book of Jeremiah in the Winchester Bible, painted at Winchester between about 1160 and 1175, showing God reaching down to touch the prophet's mouth.
sectionImages.creator: Unnamed illuminator of the Winchester Bible
sectionImages.source: Winchester Cathedral Library; photograph via Flickr and Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
sectionImages.note: A genuine twelfth-century illumination. The scene illustrates Jeremiah 1:9, where the Lord touches the prophet's mouth and puts his words in it. The Bible was made in the priory of St Swithun, probably for Bishop Henry of Blois, and its initials are the work of at least six artists.
